entities.summary:
Cao Hong (169–232 CE) emerged as a pivotal military general during the tumultuous late Eastern Han dynasty and the ensuing Three Kingdoms period in China, serving with unwavering loyalty under his cousin, the formidable warlord Cao Cao. A member of the Cao clan, his military prowess and strategic contributions were instrumental in the consolidation of power for Cao Cao, directly paving the way for the eventual establishment of the state of Cao Wei, one of the three major powers that would redefine the political landscape of East Asia for over half a century. His career spanned decades of intense civil war, shaping the early imperial ambitions that would culminate in the Wei dynasty, fundamentally altering the course of Chinese history.

Cao Hong's career was marked by active participation in several epoch-defining conflicts. He distinguished himself early during the coalition against Dong Zhuo, notably saving Cao Cao's life during a retreat after the Battle of Bian Province in 190 CE. His strategic acumen was critical during the Battle of Guandu in 200 CE, where Cao Cao decisively defeated Yuan Shao, a victory that laid the foundation for northern unification. Later, he commanded forces in the Hanzhong Campaign (217–219 CE), a protracted struggle against Liu Bei, demonstrating resilience though ultimately facing a strategic retreat. His leadership was characterized by a combination of personal bravery on the battlefield, a pragmatic approach to logistics, and an occasional controversial reputation for avarice.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Cao Hong was a key military figure whose loyal service and battlefield contributions were instrumental in establishing the Cao Wei state, directly influencing the political and military landscape of northern China during the Three Kingdoms period. His actions helped consolidate power for Cao Cao and shaped the early dynasty.
